rationale: The hypothesis posits that PLAA deficiency can be reliably structurally distinguished from true pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) by serial morphometry showing disproportionate supratentorial cerebral atrophy and delayed myelination with secondary vermian atrophy, in contrast to primary pontine flattening or the classic dragonfly pattern of cerebellar hypoplasia. However, literature evidence reveals major caveats. First, patients harboring biallelic PLAA pathogenic variants (e.g., c.68G>T, p.Gly23Val) have been clinically and neuroradiologically classified as having pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 3, with severe cerebellar atrophy documented as early as 14 days of life, complicating the claim that infratentorial involvement is merely secondary or delayed. Second, while the 'dragonfly' sign (hemispheric flattening with relative vermis sparing) is strongly linked to TSEN54 mutations in PCH2/PCH4, it is not universal across all genetic subtypes of PCH (such as CLP1- or RARS2-associated forms). Thus, phenotypic and neuroradiologic boundaries between PLAA-related neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive microcephaly, spasticity, and brain anomalies (NDMSBA) and pontocerebellar hypoplasia overlap significantly, rendering differentiation by neuroimaging alone challenging without molecular confirmation.

evidence.text: PLAA pathogenic variants (c.68G>T, p.Gly23Val) were identified in a family previously diagnosed with pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 3 (PCH3), with brain MRI showing cerebellar atrophy as early as 14 days of age.

evidence.text: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia demonstrates broad genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity; in a national multicenter cohort of 64 PCH patients, microcephaly was found in 91.3%, abnormal neurological findings in 100%, and psychomotor retardation in 98.4%, with CLP1 being the most common causative gene rather than TSEN54.

conflicts: Patients with PLAA deficiency have presented with prominent neonatal cerebellar atrophy (evident by 14 days of age) and have been categorized clinically as pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 3 (PCH3), directly contradicting the assumption that infratentorial changes are invariably secondary, delayed, or distinct from primary PCH.

The dragonfly pattern of cerebellar hemispheric hypoplasia is strongly tied to TSEN54 mutations in PCH2/PCH4, but non-TSEN forms of PCH (such as CLP1 mutations) do not consistently display this pattern, confounding the distinction between PCH variants and PLAA deficiency on the basis of cerebellar morphology alone.

new_directions.question_text: Does quantitative serial volumetric MRI reliably differentiate PLAA-related supratentorial leukoencephalopathy with vermian loss from non-TSEN54 pontocerebellar hypoplasia subtypes (such as CLP1 and RARS2)?
new_directions.rationale: Because non-TSEN forms of PCH do not display the classic dragonfly configuration and PLAA can present with early cerebellar atrophy, rigorous quantitative volumetric cutoffs for pons-to-vermis and supratentorial-to-infratentorial ratios across longitudinal scans are required.

new_directions.question_text: What is the incidence of prenatal or neonatal (first month of life) brainstem hypoplasia versus isolated cerebral white matter signal abnormality in individuals with confirmed biallelic PLAA loss-of-function variants?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying whether ventral pontine volume is genuinely preserved at birth across all known PLAA cases will establish whether pontine biometry serves as a reliable negative discriminant.
